## Naming the series on FRED

::: {.scarlet}
**AI Prompt**

Can you help me identify these leading market indicator time series variable
names as used on the St. Louis Federal Reserve Economic Database website?
Please prepare them as a **Python** dictionary I can use in my script. I will
download these variables from FRED's public CSV endpoint, and I also want each
entry to record the series' publication frequency, because I will have to
reconcile daily, weekly, and monthly data before I can model with them.
:::

The R version of this note stored the series IDs in a named character vector
and downloaded them with `quantmod::getSymbols()`. In Python we use a
dictionary of dictionaries so that each series carries its own metadata. The
frequency field is not decoration — it is the thing that will bite us in a few
cells.

```{python}
#| label: symbols

fred_series = {
    # --- Financial Market ------------------------------------------------
    "SP500":     {"group": "Financial",  "freq": "D", "label": "S&P 500 index"},
    "T10Y3M":    {"group": "Financial",  "freq": "D", "label": "10Y - 3M Treasury spread"},
    "M2REAL":    {"group": "Financial",  "freq": "M", "label": "Real M2 money stock"},

    # --- Housing / Real Economy ------------------------------------------
    "PERMIT":    {"group": "Real",       "freq": "M", "label": "Building permits (SAAR)"},
    "HOUST":     {"group": "Real",       "freq": "M", "label": "Housing starts (SAAR)"},
    "DGORDER":   {"group": "Real",       "freq": "M", "label": "New orders: durable goods"},
    "UCOGNO":    {"group": "Real",       "freq": "M", "label": "New orders: consumer goods"},
    "AWHMAN":    {"group": "Real",       "freq": "M", "label": "Avg weekly hours, mfg"},

    # --- Labor Market -----------------------------------------------------
    "ICSA":      {"group": "Labor",      "freq": "W", "label": "Initial jobless claims (SA)"},
    "TEMPHELPS": {"group": "Labor",      "freq": "M", "label": "Temporary help services (SA)"},

    # --- Sentiment --------------------------------------------------------
    "UMCSENT":   {"group": "Sentiment",  "freq": "M", "label": "U. Michigan consumer sentiment"},

    # --- Composite --------------------------------------------------------
    "USSLIND":   {"group": "Composite",  "freq": "M", "label": "Leading Index for the U.S."},
}

catalog = pd.DataFrame(fred_series).T
catalog.index.name = "series_id"
catalog
```

## Downloading from FRED

FRED publishes every series at a public CSV endpoint that needs no API key, and
the course module `fred_tools.py` wraps it. We use `fred_frame`, which fetches
each series **independently** and reports what happened. That matters: a single
bulk request for a dozen identifiers fails entirely if any one of them is
misspelled or retired, which is a poor way to learn that one identifier was
wrong.

```{python}
#| label: download

START = "1990-01-01"

raw, status = fred_frame(fred_series.keys(), start=START)

if raw.empty:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "No series could be retrieved, and the cache in data/raw/ is empty.\n"
        "This note reads from a local cache so it never depends on a live\n"
        "network at render time. Populate it once with:\n"
        "    Rscript tools/seed_fred_cache.R\n"
        "then render again."
    )

status.drop(columns=["detail"])
```

Two things in that table are worth stopping on.

First, check the `first` column against the `START` date we asked for. We
requested 1990, but FRED does not serve 1990 for every series — `SP500`, for
instance, is only distributed with a rolling ten-year window. **The start date
you request is a ceiling, not a guarantee**, and a model that silently uses
whatever it got back will be fit on a much shorter sample than you intended.

Second, any row marked `FAILED` is a series that FRED no longer publishes
under that ID. Retired IDs are a normal fact of life with FRED, and the reason
`fred_frame` fetches one at a time instead of making one bulk call. The
`detail` column, which we hid above, carries the specific error for each.

```{python}
#| label: raw-frame

print(f"{raw.shape[0]:,} rows x {raw.shape[1]} series")
print(f"Index spans {raw.index.min().date()} to {raw.index.max().date()}")
raw.tail(8)
```

That tail looks alarming — almost every cell is `NaN`. It is not an error. It
is what an outer join across mixed publication frequencies looks like: the
daily series create a row for every business day, and the monthly series have
a value on only one of those rows per month.

## Reconciling the frequencies

This is the step the R note never had to confront, because it stopped before
downloading. Any model using these indicators together needs them on one
clock. The defensible choice is to step *down* to the slowest frequency —
monthly — rather than forward-filling monthly data onto daily rows, which
would fabricate precision the source data does not have.

How you aggregate depends on what the series measures:

- **Levels and indexes** (`SP500`, `T10Y3M`, `UMCSENT`, `AWHMAN`) — take the
  monthly *mean*, which is the standard convention for converting a
  high-frequency level to a monthly observation.
- **Flows** (`ICSA`, initial claims) — these are counts accumulated over a
  week, so a monthly *sum* is the meaningful aggregate.
- **Already monthly** — leave alone.

```{python}
#| label: monthly

SUM_SERIES = {"ICSA"}

available = [c for c in raw.columns]
monthly = pd.DataFrame(index=raw.resample("MS").mean().index)

for sid in available:
    s = raw[sid].dropna()
    if fred_series[sid]["freq"] == "M":
        m = s.resample("MS").last()
    elif sid in SUM_SERIES:
        m = s.resample("MS").sum()
    else:
        m = s.resample("MS").mean()
    monthly[sid] = m

monthly = monthly.dropna(how="all")
print(f"{monthly.shape[0]:,} monthly rows x {monthly.shape[1]} series")
monthly.tail(6)
```

```{python}
#| label: coverage
#| fig-cap: "Non-missing observations by series, monthly frequency."

coverage = monthly.notna().sum().sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.barh(coverage.index, coverage.values, color=UNLV_SCARLET, alpha=0.85)
ax.set_xlabel("months of data")
ax.set_title("How much history do we actually have?")
for y, v in enumerate(coverage.values):
    ax.text(v, y, f" {v:,}", va="center", fontsize=8, color=UNLV_GRAY)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The complete-case sample — the rows where *every* series is present — is the
binding constraint on any model that uses all of them at once:

```{python}
#| label: complete-cases

complete = monthly.dropna()
if len(complete):
    print(f"Complete cases: {len(complete):,} months "
          f"({complete.index.min().date()} to {complete.index.max().date()})")
else:
    print("No month has all series present.")

print("\nLongest common window if we drop the shortest series:")
trimmed = monthly.drop(columns=[coverage.index[0]]).dropna()
if len(trimmed):
    print(f"  {len(trimmed):,} months "
          f"({trimmed.index.min().date()} to {trimmed.index.max().date()})")
```

## Looking at the indicators

```{python}
#| label: small-multiples
#| fig-cap: "Leading indicators, monthly. Note the differing vertical scales and start dates."
#| fig-height: 9

cols = [c for c in monthly.columns if monthly[c].notna().any()]
ncol = 3
nrow = -(-len(cols) // ncol)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrow, ncol, figsize=(11, 2.3 * nrow), sharex=True)
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, sid in zip(axes, cols):
    s = monthly[sid].dropna()
    ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=UNLV_SCARLET)
    ax.set_title(f"{sid} — {fred_series[sid]['label']}", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

for ax in axes[len(cols):]:
    ax.set_visible(False)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Plotted on a common time axis, the differing start dates are obvious in a way
the status table only hinted at. Several of these series simply do not exist
for the early part of the window.

```{python}
#| label: correlations
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise correlation of month-over-month changes, complete cases only."

# How you measure "change" depends on what the series is.
#
# A percent change is only meaningful for a quantity that cannot be zero or
# negative. T10Y3M is a SPREAD: it crosses zero every time the yield curve
# inverts. A spread moving from -0.10 to +0.10 is not a "200% decline" -- that
# figure is arithmetic nonsense, and dividing by a value at or near zero
# produces infinities that poison everything downstream.
#
# For series that can cross zero, the meaningful change is a simple
# difference, in the series' own units.
crosses_zero = [c for c in monthly.columns if (monthly[c].dropna() <= 0).any()]

changes = pd.DataFrame(index=monthly.index)
for col in monthly.columns:
    if col in crosses_zero:
        changes[col] = monthly[col].diff()
    else:
        changes[col] = monthly[col].pct_change(fill_method=None)

changes = changes.replace([float("inf"), float("-inf")], float("nan"))

print(f"Percent changes : {[c for c in monthly.columns if c not in crosses_zero]}")
print(f"Differences     : {crosses_zero}  (these cross zero)")

corr = changes.corr(min_periods=24)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
im = ax.imshow(corr.values, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(corr)), corr.index, fontsize=8)
ax.grid(visible=False)
for i in range(len(corr)):
    for j in range(len(corr)):
        v = corr.values[i, j]
        if pd.notna(v):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                    color="white" if abs(v) > 0.55 else "#333333")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="correlation")
ax.set_title("Correlation of monthly percent changes")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Correlating the *changes* rather than the levels matters here. Most of these
series trend, and correlating trending levels will report near-perfect
relationships between quantities that have nothing to do with one another.

But "change" is not one thing. For an index or a level that stays positive, a
percent change is the natural measure. For a **spread**, it is meaningless:
`T10Y3M` is the gap between two yields and it goes negative whenever the curve
inverts. Ask for a percent change there and you get figures like "-200%" for a
move from -0.10 to +0.10, plus an infinity every time the denominator touches
zero. One bad column is enough to make the entire correlation matrix
uncomputable.

::: {.scarlet}
Before transforming a variable, ask what it measures. A ratio, a level, a
spread, and a count do not all admit the same operations, and the code will
not stop you from applying the wrong one.
:::

## What to take from this

1. The series IDs are the easy part. Reconciling **frequency** and
   **coverage** is where the actual work is, and it is invisible until you
   download.
2. `start=` is a request, not a promise. Always verify the window you got.
3. Aggregate flows by summing and levels by averaging — the choice is
   determined by what the series measures, not by convenience.
4. Correlate changes, not levels, unless you have a reason to do otherwise.
